catalog_quote: 2.3 The suprasegmental: tone and its phonotactics The significant suprasegmental in Ejagham is tone (or pitch). Length does not have a significant lexical function in WE. In the Eyumojok-Ndebaya sub-dialect and other sub-dialects of WE, long vowels do occur in imperative forms of certain -CV verb roots, but these may be analyzed as two vowels separated by a morpheme boundary. ... Neither stress nor intonation have a significant function in the language in distinguishing syntactic or semantic categories. A given utterance can be described simply in terms of the interaction of the various lexical tones found in the given utterance and certain processes of tonal assimilation, deletion and downdrift.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Ejagham is not in the catalog. The single title-sweep item, Bendor-Samuel 1966 'Grammatical prosodies??' (Appendix IV of Pike ed., Tagmemic and matrix linguistics applied to selected African languages, pp. 192-196; Glottolog 70818), was already on file in the ERIC ED010547 full text and was read in full: it is a theoretical note on Firthian-style 'grammatical prosodies' (noun-class concord in Etung, subordinating particles and final low tone in Bimoba, English 'and') and says nothing about word stress; its Glottolog 'Suprasegmentals' tag is misleading. The only stress passages in that volume (pp. 257, 276) belong to Appendix IX on Legbo, not Etung. Nothing new was fetched sources; the best first-hand stress statement for the language remains Watters 1981 p. 50 (PDF p. 69, page image verified this sweep): 'The significant suprasegmental in Ejagham is tone... Neither stress nor intonation have a significant function in the language', i.e. a tone-only language with no functional word stress. one Glottolog fetch confirmed the bibliographic record (SIL bib 10241, lgcode etu). Records appended to Nothing remains to acquire.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ejagham is a tone language (three surface level tones plus contours, lexical and grammatical tone); the author states that stress (and intonation) has no significant/distinctive function, and gives no rule for stress placement -- prosody is described entirely in terms of lexical tone and tonal processes (assimilation, deletion, downdrift).
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Vowel length noted as non-lexical in WE; surface long vowels in some imperatives analysed as V+V across a morpheme boundary.)
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the language/utterance generally, not a word-level placement rule; sections 2.3.1-2.3.2 (pp. 51ff.) go on to describe lexical and grammatical tone, three level and three contour surface tones.
new_statements.identity_note: Watters 1981 describes the northern sub-dialect of Western Ejagham (WE, the 'Etung' area), based on the speech of the villages Eyumojok and Ndebaya, Manyu Division, Cameroon (ch.1 pp.15-16), with comparative notes on Eastern Ejagham (Keaka/Obang) and other sub-dialects. Same language as Glottolog ejag1239 'Ejagham' (ISO etu); older literature calls it Etung or Ekoi.

new_statements.reading: Ejagham (Western Ejagham, Eyumojok-Ndebaya sub-dialect, Manyu Division, Cameroon) is a tone language with no functional word stress: the author states outright that stress plays no significant role; no stress-placement rule is given anywhere in the phonology chapters (nothing on 'stress'/'accent' in the scanned chapters 1-3). Coding implication: tone-only / no word stress ('none' or 'not applicable' kind), with the caveat that this is a functional-load statement, not a phonetic study of prominence.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3 p.50: the significant suprasegmental is tone (or pitch); length not lexically significant in WE; 'Neither stress nor intonation have a significant function in the language in distinguishing syntactic or semantic categories'; utterances described purely by lexical tones plus tonal assimilation, deletion and downdrift. No other mention of stress/accent in ch.1, ch.2 (incl. notes) or the opening of 3.2.
